title: Advanced composting
teaches: Running a hot heap through its temperature stages, slower methods such as leaf mould, worm bins and bokashi, and testing whether compost is finished

blocks.text: Lesson 4 showed that a heap of balanced browns and greens, kept damp and turned now and then, heats up and rots quickly. Gardeners who follow a heap with a long compost thermometer find that it passes through the same series of stages every time, and that each stage is run by a different set of microbes. Once you can recognize the stages, you can tell a heap that is working from one that has stalled and choose the right fix for it.

In the first two or three days, everyday soil bacteria and fungi that grow best at moderate temperatures, known as **mesophiles**, feed on sugars and proteins and start to warm the core. Once the core passes about 40 degrees C, these microbes slow down and heat-loving **thermophiles** take over.[^thermophiles] The thermophilic stage is the hottest and fastest part of composting, holding the core between 50 and 65 degrees C for days or weeks, and it is the stage that kills weed seeds and plant diseases. As the easily digested food runs out, the heap cools back through the 40s, fungi return to work on the tougher cellulose and lignin, and worms, mites, and springtails move in from the edges. The last stage, called **curing**, lasts one to two months, during which the compost settles and darkens and the compounds that would harm young roots break down.

The heat comes from microbes breathing, and every meal they digest uses oxygen. In an active heap, the core can use up the oxygen in its pores within a day or two, after which the microbes rely on the little fresh air that seeps in from the surface. Turning the heap with a fork brings air back into the middle and moves the cooler outer layers into the hot core, which is why a turned heap heats up again within a day or so of each turning. The figure below models the core of a well-balanced heap so that you can change its size, its moisture, and how often it is turned.[^heatmodel]

blocks.task: Find a size, moisture and turning schedule that keeps the core above 55 degrees C for at least ten days

blocks.text: A heap much smaller than 1 m across loses heat through its sides almost as fast as its microbes make it, so it stays warm instead of becoming hot. A dry heap barely warms at all, because microbes live in thin films of water on each particle and stop feeding when those films dry out. A soggy heap heats briefly and then turns cold and sour once water has filled the pores that should hold air. Even when the core of an unturned heap runs hot, the outer 15 cm or so stays too cool to kill seeds, so weeds sprout from the finished compost. Commercial composters who must kill disease organisms reliably have to keep a turned windrow at 55 degrees C or more for at least 15 days with at least five turnings,[^rule] and a garden heap needs similar care to give the same result.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A hot heap warms through a mesophilic stage, peaks in a thermophilic stage of 50 to 65 degrees C, cools as its easily digested food runs out, and then cures for one to two months.
A heap needs to be about 1 m across or larger, as damp as a wrung-out sponge, and turned regularly to keep its core hot for more than a few days.
Turning brings fresh air to the core and moves the cool outer layers into the middle, so that every part of the heap spends time in the heat.

blocks.text: A hot heap has to be built in one go, because a pile that grows a bucket at a time never holds enough fresh food at once to heat up. Most gardeners manage this by saving materials for a few weeks, storing bags of autumn leaves and straw to mix with a load of grass clippings, a weekend of weeding, or a trailer of stable manure.

blocks.title: Building and turning a hot heap
points: Gather enough material to fill a bin about 1 m across in a single session, mixing roughly two to three buckets of browns for every bucket of greens as you go.
Chop coarse stems and tear cardboard into pieces smaller than about 5 cm. Microbes feed on surfaces, and small pieces give them far more surface to work on.

Push a compost thermometer with a 50 cm stem into the middle every day or two. Turn the heap when the core falls below about 45 degrees C after its peak, and also turn it if the core climbs above 70 degrees C, since heat that high kills even the thermophiles and stalls the heap.

Check the moisture each time you turn by squeezing a handful from the middle, which should release one or two drops of water between your fingers. Spray dry layers with a hose as you fork them over, and mix dry browns into soggy ones.

Fine white threads or a grey, ash-like coating in the hot layers are **actinomycetes**, a group of bacteria that grow as branching filaments and break down tough woody material. They show that the heap is working well.

blocks.text: Most gardens produce waste a little at a time, and many gardeners add a bucket of scraps to a bin every few days. A heap built gradually like this stays cool or only slightly warm, takes nine months to a year and a half to rot, and needs no turning, although weed seeds and disease spores in it survive. Keep seeding weeds, diseased plants, and the roots of perennial weeds out of a cool heap, or drown them in a lidded bucket of water for a month first so that they rot into a sludge that is safe to add.

blocks.caption: Months until each kind of compost is ready to use, with the main strength or limit of each method

blocks.text: Autumn leaves rot by a different route when kept on their own. Leaves contain little nitrogen and a lot of lignin, so bacteria make slow progress on them and fungi do most of the work instead. Packed damp into a wire cage or a plastic sack with a few holes punched in it, leaves turn into dark, crumbly **leaf mould** in one to two years.[^leafmould] Leaf mould is low in nutrients but holds several times its own weight in water, which makes it an excellent mulch and a good ingredient for seed and potting mixes.

A worm bin relies on compost worms such as *Eisenia fetida*, known as the tiger worm or red wiggler, which live in rotting leaf litter and manure on the surface of the ground. They are a different species from the earthworms that burrow through garden soil (Lesson 3), and they do poorly if buried in a bed.[^worms] Kept in a box of damp shredded cardboard at about 15 to 25 degrees C and fed small amounts of kitchen scraps, about half a kilogram of worms turns scraps into fine, rich castings, called **vermicompost**, in three to six months. Feed them only as much as they can finish in a few days, because a thick layer of uneaten scraps runs out of air, turns sour, and can heat the bin past 30 degrees C, which is warm enough to start killing the worms.

**Bokashi** preserves kitchen scraps by fermenting them, much as cabbage is pickled into sauerkraut. Scraps, including cooked food, meat, and dairy that would draw rats to an open heap, are pressed into an airtight bucket in layers with bran soaked in lactic acid bacteria and yeasts. Over about two weeks, the bacteria turn the scraps into a sour, pickled mass with a pH near 4, and the liquid that collects at the bottom is drained off through a tap every few days. The fermented scraps still look like scraps, so they have to be buried in a trench in the garden or mixed into a compost heap, where soil life breaks them down within two to four weeks. Wait about two weeks before planting into a trench of fresh bokashi, because its acidity can damage young roots until soil life has digested it.

Compost that has finished its hot stage still needs to cure before it goes near seedlings. Immature compost can contain ammonia and organic acids that stunt germinating seeds, and the microbes still feeding on its leftover carbon can pull nitrogen out of the soil around young roots, just as the dug-in sawdust did in Lesson 4. Finished compost is dark brown and crumbly, smells like damp woodland, has cooled to the temperature of the air, and stays cool when it is turned and watered.

Two simple home tests check maturity more closely. For the reheating test, moisten a bucket of compost, mix it well, and push a thermometer into the middle; if it warms more than a few degrees above the air temperature within three days, the microbes are still feeding and the compost needs more time. For the cress test, fill one small pot with your compost and another with bought seed compost, sow 20 cress seeds on the surface of each, and keep both moist on a windowsill.[^cress] After five days, count the seedlings in each pot and compare the length of their roots. If the seeds in your compost are clearly fewer or stunted, leave the heap to cure for another month and test it again.

blocks.title: Try it in the garden
points: The next time you build a heap, push a thermometer into its core every day for the first two weeks and write down the readings. Turn the heap once the temperature starts to fall, and check whether it climbs again over the following two days.
Run a cress test on your compost before using it to sow seeds, alongside a pot of bought seed compost for comparison.
If you have no room for a hot heap, fill a few sacks with damp autumn leaves for leaf mould next year, or set up a worm bin in a shed or garage for your kitchen scraps.

items.question: A heap's core reaches 62 degrees C in its first week, then falls to 40 degrees C by the end of the second, although plenty of material is still unrotted. What is the most likely cause?
options: The microbes have used up the oxygen in the core, and turning the heap will bring the heat back
The compost is finished and ready to spread on seedlings
The heap has too many browns and needs no further care
items.why: In an active heap, the oxygen in the core runs out within days. Turning brings fresh air into the middle, and a heap with food left in it heats up again within a day or two.

items.question: Why does a heap only 50 cm across rarely get hot, even with a well-balanced mix?
options: It loses heat through its sides almost as fast as its microbes make it
Small heaps always have the wrong carbon-to-nitrogen ratio
Heat-loving microbes cannot live in small heaps
items.why: A heap makes heat throughout its volume but loses it through its surface, and a small heap has far more surface for its volume. Heaps about 1 m across or larger hold enough heat to pass 55 degrees C.

items.question: Why can weed seeds survive in a heap whose core ran hot, if the heap was never turned?
options: The outer layers of the heap never got hot enough to kill them
Weed seeds are unharmed by any compost temperature
Heat in the core makes seeds sprout faster
items.why: The outer 15 cm or so of a heap stays much cooler than the core. Turning moves that outer material into the middle so that it also spends time above 55 degrees C.

items.question: You squeeze a handful of material from the middle of a hot heap. What should happen if the moisture is right?
options: One or two drops of water appear between your fingers
A stream of water runs down your wrist
It falls apart as dry dust
items.why: Material as damp as a wrung-out sponge has water films for microbes to live in and open pores for air. A stream of water means the pores are flooded, and dust means the microbes have dried out.

items.question: Which worms belong in a worm bin?
options: Surface-dwelling compost worms such as Eisenia fetida, the tiger worm or red wiggler
Large earthworms dug out of the vegetable bed
Any worms at all, as long as the bin is kept hot
items.why: Compost worms live naturally in rotting litter and manure and thrive in a crowded bin. Burrowing garden earthworms need mineral soil and do poorly in a bin.

items.question: After two weeks in a bokashi bucket, what do the fermented scraps need before they can feed plants?
options: Burying in the soil or mixing into a heap, where soil life breaks them down over a few weeks
Nothing, since they can be used as potting mix straight away
Drying in the sun for a month
items.why: Fermentation pickles the scraps without breaking them down. Soil organisms finish the job within two to four weeks once the scraps are buried or added to a heap.

items.question: Why do autumn leaves kept on their own take one to two years to turn into leaf mould?
options: They are low in nitrogen and high in lignin, so slow-working fungi do most of the decay
Leaves contain chemicals that kill every microbe
Leaves have to freeze solid before they can rot
items.why: With little nitrogen, bacteria cannot multiply quickly on leaves, and the lignin in them is broken down mainly by fungi, which work slowly.

items.question: Cress seeds sown in your compost sprout poorly and grow short roots compared with seeds in bought seed compost. What does that tell you?
options: The compost is immature and should cure for longer
The compost has been stored too long and lost its value
Cress is unable to grow in any compost
items.why: Immature compost contains ammonia and organic acids that harm germinating seeds. Another month or two of curing gives soil life time to break these compounds down.

summary: **A hot heap goes through stages.** It warms, peaks at 50 to 65 °C, cools as easy food runs out, then cures for one to two months.
**The heat kills weed seeds and diseases.** Only a properly hot heap does that.
**Hot heaps need size, water and air.** Build one batch about 1 m across, damp as a wrung-out sponge, with small pieces, and turn it when the core cools.
**Turning keeps every part in the heat.** It brings air to the core and moves the cool outside into the middle.
**Slower methods work with less material.** Cool heaps, leaf mould, worm bins and bokashi all make good compost, but none kills weed seeds.
**Test before you sow.** Finished compost is dark, crumbly and earthy, stays cool after turning, and passes a cress germination test.

thermophiles.title: Thermophiles and actinomycetes
thermophiles.text: Microbes that grow best between about 45 and 70 degrees C are called **thermophiles**. In a compost heap they include *Bacillus* and *Thermus* bacteria and the **actinomycetes**, bacteria that grow as fine branching threads. Actinomycetes also make geosmin, the compound that gives finished compost and freshly dug soil their earthy smell. Most thermophiles survive in ordinary soil and on plant material as dormant spores or small, inactive populations, and they multiply rapidly once a heap warms up enough to suit them.

heatmodel.title: Modelling a heap's heat
heatmodel.text: The figure follows the core of a well-balanced heap one day at a time. Each day, the microbes eat in proportion to the food left, the oxygen in the core, and how well the core temperature suits them, with the fastest work between about 55 and 62 degrees C and a steep fall above that. Eating warms the core and uses up oxygen, while the heap's surface sheds heat and lets fresh air seep back in, both faster for a small heap than a large one. Turning restores all the oxygen at once and releases some heat. The rates were tuned by hand to match the pattern reported for garden and farm heaps, so the curves show how size, moisture, and turning interact without predicting the exact temperatures of any real heap.

rule.title: Pathogen rules for commercial compost
rule.text: In the United States, the federal rules for composting sewage sludge (40 CFR Part 503), which many state rules for other composts follow, require a turned windrow to stay at 55 degrees C or more for at least 15 days with at least five turnings. A static pile that has air blown through it and is insulated under a layer of finished compost or wood chips only has to stay at that temperature for three days, because the insulation keeps its outer layers almost as hot as its core.

leafmould.title: Choosing leaves for leaf mould
leafmould.text: Thin leaves such as oak, beech, and hornbeam rot into fine leaf mould within a year or two, while thicker leaves such as sycamore and horse chestnut take longer. Tough evergreen leaves such as holly and laurel can take several years and are better shredded and added to the compost heap. Running a lawn mower over a pile of leaves before bagging them chops them into small pieces and mixes in a little grass, which noticeably speeds up the rotting.

worms.title: Compost worms and earthworms
worms.text: Earthworms fall into three groups by where they live. Litter dwellers such as *Eisenia fetida* live in the top few centimetres of rotting leaves and manure, breed quickly, and tolerate crowding, which is why they suit a worm bin. Topsoil dwellers make shallow, branching burrows and feed on soil and the organic matter in it. Deep burrowers such as *Lumbricus terrestris* dig vertical burrows a metre or more deep and drag fallen leaves down from the surface, so they need undisturbed soil and starve in a bin.

cress.title: The cress germination test
cress.text: Garden cress, *Lepidium sativum*, sprouts within a day or two and is sensitive to the ammonia, organic acids, and salts found in immature compost, so laboratories use it to measure compost maturity. In the laboratory version described by Zucconi and colleagues in 1981, seeds are germinated on a water extract of the compost and compared with seeds on pure water, and the result combines the share of seeds that sprouted with the length of their roots into a germination index. Compost that is rich in nutrients can slow cress slightly even when it is mature, because of its salts, so the home test is most useful for spotting compost that is clearly unready.
